Evidence of Property Ownership in Inheritance Division In a lawsuit for the dissolution of an inheritance community among siblings, the plaintiff sought the division of real estate inherited from their parents. The legal issue concerns the burden of proof regarding property title within the framework of "scioglimento della comunione". The interpretative problem lies in determining whether administrative documents are sufficient to establish ownership. The Court applied the principle that inheritance tax returns and cadastral surveys are insufficient to prove legal ownership, as they lack the evidentiary weight of property deeds and do not confirm the actual transfer of rights from the deceased to the heirs.
 Impact of Building Irregularities on Judicial Division The litigation involved buildings constructed without necessary permits, including a warehouse and a covered terrace, which were deemed non-remediable by a court expert. The legal classification pertains to urban planning compliance in judicial proceedings. The core interpretative challenge was whether an inheritance could be divided if it contained illegal structures. Following the Supreme Court Joint Sessions (n. 25021/2019), the Court ruled that judicial division is prohibited for properties with building irregularities unless the claim is specifically limited to the legally compliant portions of the estate.
 Necessary Participation of All Successors The facts revealed the existence of a deceased brother whose potential successors were neither identified nor summoned. This involves the legal principle of "litisconsorzio necessario" (necessary joinder) in inheritance dissolution. The interpretative problem arises when the exact shares of the property are uncertain due to missing heirs. The Court determined that failure to clarify the succession chain of all original heirs makes it impossible to define the ownership quotas correctly, leading to the rejection of the division clai.
